topics.title: The Miraculous Night Journey from Makkah to the Farthest Mosque in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: The last days of the Makkan phase of the Prophet's life are noted for alternate fortunes ranging between two extremes: gradual success and continual persecution. However, glimpses of propitious lights were looming on the distant horizon, to ultimately materialize in the event of the Prophet's Night Journey to Jerusalem and then Ascension through the spheres of the heavens. As for its exact date, it is still controversial and no common consent has been reached; however, the majority of jurists is in favour of a date between 16 and 12 months prior to migration to Madinah. The following is an epitome of the details of that miraculous event narrated on the authority of Ibn Al-Qayyim.

The Messenger of Allah (Peace be upon him) was carried in body from the Sacred Mosque in Makkah to the Distant Mosque in Jerusalem on a horse called Al-Buraq, in the company of Gabriel, the archangel. There he alighted, tethered the horse to a ring in the gate of the Mosque and led the Prophets in prayer. After that Gabriel took him to the heavens on the same horse.

When they reached the first heaven, Gabriel asked the guardian angel to open the door. It was opened and he saw Adam, the progenitor of mankind. The Prophet (Peace be upon him) saluted him and Adam welcomed him and expressed his faith in Muhammad's Prophethood. He saw the souls of martyrs on his right and those of the wretched on his left. Gabriel then ascended with the Prophet to the second heaven, where he saw and saluted John, son of Zachariah (Yahya bin Zakariya), and Jesus, son of Mary; they returned the salutation and expressed their faith in his Prophethood.

Then they reached the third heaven where they saw and saluted Joseph (Yusuf), who welcomed him and expressed faith in his Prophethood. In the fourth heaven he met the Prophet Enoch (Idris) and saluted him, and Idris returned the salutation. In the fifth heaven he met the Prophet Aaron (Harun), who returned the salutation and expressed faith in his Prophethood.

In the sixth heaven he met Moses (Musa) and saluted him; the latter returned the salutation. On the Prophet (Peace be upon him) leaving, he saw that Moses began to weep. He asked the reason. Moses answered that he was weeping because he witnessed a man sent after him as a Messenger (Muhammad) who was able to lead more of his people to Paradise than he himself did. Then the Prophet (Peace be upon him) reached the seventh heaven and met Abraham (Ibrahim), who returned the salutation and expressed faith in his Prophethood.

Then he was carried to Sidrat-al-Muntaha (the remotest lote tree) and was shown Al-Bait-al-Ma'mûr [(the much frequented house) which is like the Ka'bah, encompassed daily by seventy thousand angels, so that the angels who once encompassed it would not have their turn again till the Resurrection]. He was then presented to the Divine Presence and experienced the thrill of witnessing the Divine Glory and Manifestation at the closest possible propinquity. There the Lord revealed unto His servant that which He revealed, and ordained fifty daily prayers for him.

On his return, he spoke to Moses that his followers had been enjoined to pray fifty times a day. Moses said: "Your followers cannot perform so many prayers. Go back to your Lord and ask for a remission in number." The Prophet (Peace be upon him) turned to Gabriel as if holding counsel with him; Gabriel nodded, "Yes, if you desire," and ascended with him to the Presence of Allah. Allah made a reduction of ten prayers. He then descended and reported that to Moses, who again urged him to request a further reduction. He went again and again, at Moses' suggestion, until the prayers were reduced to five only. Moses again asked him to implore for more, but he said: "I feel ashamed now of repeatedly asking my Lord for reduction. I accept and resign to His Will." When Muhammad (Peace be upon him) went farther, a Caller was heard saying: "I have imposed My Ordinance and alleviated the burden of My servants."

There is some difference as regards whether the Prophet saw Allah with his physical eye or not. Some interpreters say that seeing Allah with his naked eyes was not confirmed. Ibn 'Abbas, on the other hand, says that the word Ru'ya as used in the Noble Qur'ân signifies observation with the help of the eye. In Sûrah An-Najm we read: "Then he approached and came closer." [53:8] Here 'he' refers to the archangel Gabriel, and this context is completely different from that in the Prophetic tradition of Isra' and Mi'raj, where 'the approach' relates to that of the Lord, Glory be to Him.

Some significant incidents featured the 'Night Journey' of the Prophet, of which we could mention: The Prophet's breast was cleft by Gabriel, his heart extracted and washed with the water of Zamzam. There were also brought to him two gold vessels, one full of milk and the other of wine; he was asked to choose, and selected the milk and drank it. The angel said: "You have been guided on Al-Fitrah; had you selected wine, your nation would have been misled." [Al-Fitrah denotes the original, unspoilt natural disposition.]

The Prophet told that he saw two manifest rivers — the Nile and the Euphrates — and two hidden ones. The two manifest rivers symbolically describe the fertile area in which Muhammad's Message will settle, whose people will always remain the bearers of Islam, passed on from generation to generation. He also saw Malik, the guardian of Hell, with a cheerless frowning face. Therein he saw the Hell-dwellers, of whom were those who unjustly devour the property of orphans, having flews like those of camels and swallowing red-hot stones; the people who take usury, with bellies too big to move, trodden by the people of Pharaoh; the adulterers offered tasty meat and rotten meat but choosing the rotten; and the licentious women hanging by their breasts.

The 'Night Journey' raised a good deal of stir among the people, and the sceptical audience plied Muhammad with all sorts of questions. He told them he had seen the camels of Makkan merchants to and fro, guided them to some of their stray animals, and informed them that he had drunk some of their water while they were asleep and left the container covered. The disbelievers pestered him with questions about the description of the Mosque at Jerusalem, where he had never gone before; to the astonishment of many, his replies furnished the most accurate information. Yet all this increased in them nothing but flight from the Truth and disbelief.

For the true Muslims, however, there was nothing unusual about the Night Journey. The All-Mighty Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth by an act of His Will, is surely Powerful enough to take His Messenger beyond the heavens and show him His signs at first hand. The disbelievers went to see Abu Bakr on account of this event, and he readily said: "Yes, I do verify it." It was on this occasion that he earned the title of As-Siddiq (the verifier of the truth).

The most eloquent and most concise justification of this Journey is expressed in Allah's Words: "...in order that We might show him (Muhammad) of Our Ayât (proofs, evidences, signs)." [17:1] The Divine rule regarding the Prophets is: "Thus did We show Abraham the kingdom of the heavens and the earth that he be one of those who have Faith with certainty." [6:75] To Moses, his Lord said: "That We may show you (some) of Our Greater Signs." [20:23] The Prophets, after seeing Allah's Signs, establish their Faith on solid certainty too immune to be parted with, for they are the ones who will bear burdens too heavy for ordinary people to carry.

The story of the Night Journey in the Noble Qur'ân is epitomised in the first verse of Sûrah Al-Isra' (Chapter 17), then there is a quick shift to uncover the crimes of the Jews, followed by an admonition that the Qur'ân guides to that which is most just. This is not coincidental. Jerusalem was the first scene of the Night Journey, and here lies the message to the Jews: that they would be discharged of the office of leadership of mankind due to their crimes, and that this office would be reinstituted by the Messenger of Allah (Peace be upon him), holding in his hand both headquarters of the Abrahamic Faith — the Holy Sanctuary in Makkah and the Farthest Mosque in Jerusalem. It was high time for spiritual authority to be transferred from a nation pregnant with treachery and covenant-breaching to another blessed with piety and dutifulness.

There remains a crucial question: how could this foreseen transition of authority be effected while the champion himself was left deserted in the hillocks of Makkah? This uncovered a new phase of the Islamic Call. Its forerunners took the shape of Qur'ânic verses of unequivocal warning to the polytheists: "And when We decide to destroy a town, We (first) send a definite order to those among them who are given the good things of this life. Then they transgress therein, and thus the word (of torment) is justified against it. Then We destroy it with complete destruction. And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah! And Sufficient is your Lord as an All-Knower and All-Beholder of the sins of His slaves." [17:16-17] Together with these, other verses were revealed showing the Muslims the rules of the civilization upon which they could erect their community, foreshadowing their ownership of a land and a secure shelter from which to communicate the Message to the world — that was the inner secret of that blessed journey. For this wisdom we deem it appropriate to suggest that the Night Journey took place either before the First Pledge of 'Aqabah or between the two; after all, Allah knows best.

topics.topicSummary: In the late Makkan period, the Prophet ﷺ was taken bodily by night on the Buraq from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque in Jerusalem, where he led the Prophets in prayer, then ascended through the seven heavens — greeting Adam, Yahya & Jesus, Yusuf, Idris, Harun, Musa and Ibrahim — to Sidrat-al-Muntaha and the Divine Presence, where fifty daily prayers were ordained and, at Moses' urging, reduced to five. He chose milk over wine (a sign of Fitrah) and witnessed scenes of Paradise and Hell. The disbelievers mocked, but Abu Bakr's instant verification earned him the title As-Siddiq.
keyPoints: The Prophet ﷺ was carried bodily on the Buraq from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque (Jerusalem) with Gabriel
He led the Prophets in prayer in Jerusalem, then ascended through the seven heavens
He greeted Adam, Yahya & Jesus, Yusuf, Idris, Harun, Musa and Ibrahim in the heavens
At Sidrat-al-Muntaha and the Divine Presence, fifty daily prayers were ordained, then reduced to five at Moses' repeated urging
He chose the vessel of milk over wine — a sign of Al-Fitrah (the natural disposition)
He witnessed Paradise, and Hell with its dwellers (devourers of orphans' wealth, usurers, adulterers)
Abu Bakr instantly believed the event, earning the title As-Siddiq (the verifier of truth)
Surah Al-Isra' [17:1] signals the transfer of spiritual leadership from a treacherous nation to the believers

quiz.question: On what was the Prophet ﷺ carried during the Night Journey?
How many daily prayers were finally prescribed after the reductions urged by Moses?
Who earned the title 'As-Siddiq' for instantly verifying the Night Journey?
When the Prophet ﷺ was offered milk and wine, which did he choose and what did it signify?
options: Milk — a sign of Al-Fitrah (the natural disposition)
quiz.answer: Milk — a sign of Al-Fitrah (the natural disposition)
